children: By David S. Cloud and Anat Peled

TEL AVIV-Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu revels in his annual appearances before the United Nations General Assembly, defiantly excoriating the world body. In 2024, he called it a "house of darkness" and a "swamp of antisemitic bile."
But this year, Netanyahu's speech shined a light on something very different: his isolation.

The weakened Israeli leader addressed the U.N. on Thursday weeks before he faces elections that cap a turbulent period marked by the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attacks from Gaza and nearly three years of wars. He arrived in the U.S. hours before his speech and is set to depart shortly after.
As Netanyahu took the podium, dozens of delegates walked out of the chamber, repeating a protest many also staged when he spoke last year.

Netanyahu responded with a defiant defense of Israel's three-year-old multi-front war, calling the absent delegates "moral cowards" and rejecting accusations that its aggressive military tactics amounted to genocide in Gaza. He held up a pager in a reminder of the 2024 attack on Hezbollah operatives that used explosives hidden in the devices.
His message was primarily aimed at Israelis who will vote next month on whether to replace him as prime minister.
"To all the heroes of Israel, I pledge a sacred vow: We will continue to defend our state. We will continue to win because we have no other choice," he said.

For Netanyahu, the annual U.N. gathering has been a favorite forum to warn of the risks of a nuclear-armed Iran and to trumpet his political clout in the U.S. But neither will be an easy sell this time. Since his U.N. speech last year, Iran has survived a monthslong joint U.S.-Israeli air campaign and Netanyahu's stock, even among Israel's supporters in the U.S., is at a nadir.

"Netanyahu has found himself over the years in a lot of corners," said Avishay Ben Sasson-Gordis, head of U.S.-Israel research at the Institute for National Security Studies, an Israeli think tank. "But this is potentially the sharpest one, and he is with his back to the wall."

Netanyahu had sought a meeting with President Trump during this week's gathering, but nothing has materialized, people familiar with the matter said. The prime minister and his close circle also previously hoped that Trump would lobby for him and lend him support on the campaign trail. That appears unlikely, too, as relations between the two men have deteriorated.
U.S. and Israeli officials said that the meeting didn't come together due to scheduling constraints.

But Netanyahu paid tribute to Trump in his speech, saying Israel had "no greater partner" and applauding him for attacking Iranian nuclear facilities in 2025 and ordering a joint air campaign against Tehran earlier this year.
"Israel and America acted together, not only to protect ourselves but to save civilization," he said.

He hopes to receive a boost in the polls by presenting himself as an irreplaceable figure who can defend his embattled country in polished English before the world, in a speech delivered in prime time in Israel, political analysts say.

"While he surely would have welcomed the opportunity to see President Trump, his biggest concern is trying once again to convince a skeptical Israeli public that he alone can protect the state of Israel," said Jonathan Panikoff, a former deputy U.S. intelligence officer for the Middle East now at the Atlantic Council think tank in Washington.

Even before heading to the U.N., Netanyahu and his allies escalated a feud with New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani. As recently as July, the mayor said city lawyers were studying whether they could have Netanyahu arrested under a warrant issued in 2024 by the International Criminal Court alleging he had committed war crimes in Gaza, where tens of thousands of Palestinians have been killed in the conflict with Israel.
On Tuesday, Mamdani called Netanyahu "the architect of horrific genocide against Palestinians."

Netanyahu and the Israeli government have rejected the allegations and challenged the legality of the warrant. Mamdani has acknowledged local authorities cannot execute the arrest warrant. But the clash has made him a target for Netanyahu's election campaign.
"You falsely, repeatedly accuse Israel of genocide, Mr. Mamdani. You try to stop me from coming here. You try to silence me. Well you can't silence me," Netanyahu said.

In an AI-generated election ad by the Netanyahu campaign, a gleeful, computer-generated Mamdani is shown with other Netanyahu foes-Mojtaba Khamenei, Iran's supreme leader; Recep Tayyip Erdogan, the president of Turkey; and Mahmoud Abbas, the leader of the Palestinian Authority. In the ad, when Netanyahu unexpectedly wins the election, the men call off a planned party in disappointment.
"They want Netanyahu to fall. Don't let them win," an ominous voice says.

Arab governments have used the U.N. as a forum for criticizing Israel for decades, but this year the attacks on Netanyahu's policies are even sharper. "This government's sense of impunity has reached terrifying levels," Jordan's King Abdullah II said Tuesday in a U.N. speech largely devoted to criticizing Israel.

Abbas on Thursday charged that Israeli policies are destroying the two-state solution and threatening the existence of the Palestinian people. "No lasting security can be built upon the occupation of another people, and the denial of its legitimate rights," said Abbas, who was speaking to the U.N. by video after the U.S. denied him a visa for a second year running. "We want a process that puts an end to occupation, and guarantees freedom and self-determination for Palestinians, a process that guarantees, also, security and peace for Israelis and the countries of the region," Abbas said.
Netanyahu faces tight elections, with current polling showing he would fail to secure a ruling majority in the Oct. 27 vote, as Israelis remain divided over his leadership.

Though his military moves are widely supported by many Israelis, opponents blame Netanyahu for failing to head off the Oct. 7 attacks. They also say he has weakened Israel's alliance with the U.S. and ties with other major powers.

The Trump administration earlier this month proposed a $2.8 billion arms package for Israel. But Trump's frustration with Netanyahu has boiled over at times in recent months as he has tried to end the war with Iran.

They have also clashed over Israel's bombings in Lebanon and a U.S.-backed peace plan for Gaza. Last month, Netanyahu rejected Trump's plan for a phased disarmament of Hamas and resumed airstrikes on the militants after a short pause in Israeli strikes.
The lack of a meeting between the two leaders before the Israeli elections and the U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3 reflects that tension.

"Netanyahu today is very much seen as toxic," in a way that prevents many countries engaging with Israel, said Yaakov Katz, a senior fellow at the Jewish People Policy Institute, a think tank in Jerusalem.
"Israel is more isolated today on the international stage than it's probably ever been since the beginning of the state in 1948."
